prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I have a need to ventilate, to have my porous body—sockets and holes—open to the bald-faced wind and have my heathen inner-stuff tweedled like a reed flute and this piffle floats out. But walking on the open road, I know even open roads, to be roads at all, are ruts. With a careless beanfield on either side, off one more time, even you, Mr. Out-in-the-Woods, might as well be stuffed in your hometown bucket. And if these grim beams of trees are truly home, Sweet, as you say they are, then the timberwolves would reclaim you by singing and that would be all. The Moon would reclaim the timberwolves—not a snarl—soft keepsakes asleep in the palm of Her hand. I would reclaim the Moon by picking a white silk chrysanthemum and resting it on the branch beside Her. Who would reclaim me? and say, “Blossom, we are not two. There is no road to or from. You cannot write a love poem. You cannot walk away.” Each “Appleblossom” is a verse translation from the Japanese of a short selection from the notebooks of Chiri, Bashō’s traveling companion during the years between Withered Chestnuts and Travelogue of Weatherbeaten Bones.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: But, With, Out

outputs.L1:
I need to ventilate—to open my porous body, sockets and holes, to the bald-faced wind; to have my heathen inner stuff tweedled like a reed flute, so that this piffle may float out. Yet, walking the open road, I know that even open roads, if they are to be roads at all, are ruts. And if these grim beams of trees are truly home, Sweet, as you say they are, then the timberwolves would reclaim you in song, and that would be all. The Moon would reclaim the timberwolves—not a snarl, but soft keepsakes asleep in the palm of Her hand. I would reclaim the Moon by picking a white silk chrysanthemum and resting it on the branch beside Her.

Who would reclaim me and say, “Blossom, we are not two. There is no road to or from. You cannot write a love poem. You cannot walk away”?

Each “Appleblossom” is a verse translation from the Japanese of a short selection from the notebooks of Chiri, Bashō’s traveling companion during the years between *Withered Chestnuts* and *Travelogue of Weatherbeaten Bones*.
outputs.L2:
I feel compelled to let the air pass through me—to expose every opening and hollow of this porous body to the blunt wind, so that my pagan insides whistle like reeds and release such nonsense. Yet when I travel the open road, I understand that even the freest road remains a track worn into the earth. Stray once more between indifferent beanfields, and even you, Mr. Wilderness, may as well be crammed into the pail of your native town.

And if, Sweet, these dark uprights of the forest are truly your home, as you insist, the wolves could call you back with their song, and that would end the matter. Then the Moon would gather the wolves to Herself without so much as a growl, keeping them as gentle mementos asleep in Her palm. I, in turn, would claim the Moon by plucking a white silk chrysanthemum and placing it on the branch at Her side.

But who would come to claim me and say, “Blossom, you and I are one. No path leads away or returns. A love poem is beyond your power to write. You cannot leave”?

Every piece titled “Appleblossom” is a verse rendering from Japanese, drawn from a brief selection in the journals of Chiri, who accompanied Bashō on his travels in the period between *Withered Chestnuts* and *Travelogue of Weatherbeaten Bones*.
outputs.L3:
The speaker expresses a profound need to open both body and inner self to the wind, surrendering to a force that allows language, feeling, and identity to emerge without restraint. Yet even the apparent freedom of open roads proves deceptive: they are figured as ruts, predetermined tracks that cannot offer a genuine escape from one’s origins.

Against this limited form of movement, nature is imagined as an ongoing cycle of belonging and reclamation. The forests reclaim the wolves, the wolves reclaim the Moon, and the Moon, in turn, participates in a larger pattern of return. The speaker longs to be drawn into this same unity—to be reclaimed so completely that separation and departure would no longer be possible. In such a state, even love poetry would become unnecessary, because love would no longer depend on distance, longing, or the distinction between self and other.

Each piece titled “Appleblossom” is presented as a verse translation from the Japanese notebooks of Chiri, the traveling companion of the poet Bashō. This framing gives the sequence the quality of a recovered travel record while reinforcing its central concerns with movement, nature, memory, and the desire to return to a deeper form of belonging.
outputs.L4:
The desire for freedom often begins with the dream of departure. We imagine a road leading beyond the claims of family, history, habit, and even the self. If only we could travel far enough, we think, we might arrive somewhere untouched by what we have been. Yet every landscape we enter also enters us. The road does not erase belonging; it reveals how deeply we belong—to memory, to the natural world, and to the lives through which our own life has taken shape.

This tension lies at the heart of the verse translations drawn from the Japanese notebooks of Chiri, Bashō’s traveling companion. The poems are brief, but their brevity does not make them slight. A blossom, a birdcall, a moonlit path, or the passing of a season becomes an opening through which an entire spiritual landscape can be seen. Human feeling is not placed above nature or merely projected onto it. Instead, feeling and nature arise together. The traveler’s loneliness belongs to the evening wind; the fragility of the blossom belongs to the person who pauses to see it.

Travel in these poems therefore carries a double meaning. It promises release from fixed identity, but it also exposes the impossibility of leaving oneself behind. Each step away becomes another form of return. What appears to be escape is finally a deeper encounter with the world and with the hidden continuities of the self. The traveler may abandon a house, a name, or a familiar community, but not the web of relationships that makes perception possible. To see the road is already to be joined to it.

Belonging, in this sense, is not possession. It is not the security of remaining in one place or the reassurance of being recognized by others. It is a condition of mutual presence. The self belongs to the world because it is made from the world: from weather, language, memory, loss, and attention. The world, in turn, becomes intimate through the act of noticing it. A flower is never only a symbol, but neither is it merely an object. It is itself, and it is also the moment in which observer and observed meet.

This is why there can be no true road away. Escape depends on the belief that self and world are separate, that one may withdraw from one realm and enter another unchanged. Chiri’s verses quietly undo that belief. The farther the traveler goes, the clearer it becomes that separation is provisional. Roads cross mountains and provinces, but they do not lead outside existence. Solitude may loosen social bonds, yet it cannot sever the bond between consciousness and what consciousness encounters.

For the same reason, these translations do not become love poems in the conventional sense. They offer no isolated beloved, no simple drama of longing and fulfillment. Their love is less possessive and more encompassing. It is expressed through attention: to apple blossom, rain, dust, silence, and transience. What is loved cannot be held apart from the one who loves it. Affection becomes a recognition of unity, and loss becomes an acknowledgment that every form is passing even as it remains part of a larger whole.

The name “Appleblossom” gives the translations their emblem. Apple blossom suggests beauty at the edge of disappearance, renewal inseparable from fragility, and fruit concealed within a brief flowering. The translations likewise reclaim what might otherwise remain marginal: the companion’s notebook, the traveler’s passing observation, the small natural image overshadowed by grander narratives. Reclamation here is not an attempt to possess the past. It is an act of listening that allows neglected words and perceptions to enter the present.

Their spiritual significance lies in this recovery of relationship. The poems do not offer transcendence as flight from the material world. They find it within the material world, in the instant when blossom, traveler, road, and memory cease to appear as separate things. Freedom is no longer imagined as absolute independence. It becomes freedom from the illusion of isolation.

In the end, the journey returns us to what was always true: the self is not enclosed, and the world is not outside it. There is no road away because every road passes through the same indivisible reality. There is no conventional love poem because love is not confined to one object or one human bond. The “Appleblossom” translations become meditations on unity—small acts of spiritual reclamation in which the forgotten, the transient, and the divided are gathered again into belonging.
outputs.L5:
**But, With, Out**

“But” is a turn in the road. It interrupts certainty and makes room for another possibility. “With” is companionship—a bridge between people, ideas, and moments. “Out” suggests distance, departure, or escape.

Together, they form “without,” a word that describes absence. Yet absence is not always emptiness. To live without something can reveal what truly matters; to step out can lead us toward something new; and to question with “but” can change the direction of our lives.

We move through the world with others, step out on our own, and meet countless “buts” along the way. Each small word carries a choice: to resist, to connect, or to leave.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem inspired by Bashō’s travel journals, exploring wandering, nature, love, and the paradox that even open roads are confining. End with a fictional scholarly note explaining that the “Appleblossom” pieces are translations from the notebooks of Bashō’s companion Chiri.
counterfactuals.output:
### APPLEBLOSSOM I: MILEPOST

At dawn the road unrolls its gray sleeve.

We enter it like a letter.

On the left, flooded fields borrow the sky; on the right, cedars keep their dark counsel. A heron lifts, white as an unwritten farewell. My sandals learn the grammar of stones.

I say: *To wander is to be without walls.*

You point to the mileposts.

Each one waits ahead like a small official, counting our escape.

Apple petals cross the road—  
even the wind travels  
inside its season.

---

### APPLEBLOSSOM II: THE INN AT REED MARSH

Rain fastens us to the evening.

The innkeeper gives us one lamp, two bowls, a room thin as a sleeve. Through the paper wall, frogs strike their bronze bells in the marsh. Your wet hair smells of smoke and plum bark. I do not touch it.

Love is sometimes the hand withheld, hovering above the warmth it has crossed provinces to find.

We lie side by side.

Between us: one folded robe, three unspoken names, the entire road.

Night rain—  
the bridge keeps going  
beneath our sleep.

---

### APPLEBLOSSOM III: BARRIER WITHOUT GATE

No guard. No wall. Only mountains narrowing until the path must pass through a single thought.

Here, travelers once presented documents. Now the checkpoint is abandoned. Ferns occupy the booth; a fox has signed the ledger with its tail.

Still, we lower our voices.

Still, the body remembers permission.

Beyond the barrier, the same moon. Behind it, the same moon. Yet we stand beneath the rotted beam as if divided into before and after.

You ask which side is freedom.

I answer by walking.

My shadow follows under arrest.

---

### APPLEBLOSSOM IV: LETTER NEVER SENT

Beloved—

The sea was visible today between two pines, a blue blade too far away to wound us. Bashō said distance sharpens what it cannot possess. Then he walked ahead, coughing into his sleeve.

I thought of your garden at home: the pear tree bent over the well, the gate that sticks in winter, the cup with the chipped green rim. I left these things to become boundless. Now each step ties another thread from my ankle to them.

The road does not sever.

It lengthens the cord.

Migrating geese—  
their freedom written  
in formation.

---

### APPLEBLOSSOM V: OPEN COUNTRY

For ten days, no city.

Grass, cloud, grass. A river repeatedly losing and finding itself. We sleep under pines whose roots clutch the mountain even while their needles travel everywhere.

This is called the open road.

But the road permits only forward or back. Leave it and the thorn takes your sleeve, the marsh takes your foot, the village dog takes your measure. Follow it and every bend commands: *Not here. Farther.*

How spacious the cage without bars.

How obediently the horizon moves away.

At noon, you laugh and run through the tall grass. For an instant there is no path, no master, no destination—only your blue robe rising and vanishing among seed heads.

Then you stop.

Even joy must breathe inside the body.

Summer field—  
a horse circles the stake  
of its own long shadow.

---

### APPLEBLOSSOM VI: LAST LODGING

The map ends before the land does.

We arrive at a hut where apple trees bloom out of season, or perhaps we have mistaken snow for blossoms, age for spring, return for departure. Petals gather in Bashō’s open notebook. He brushes away none of them.

Tonight the moon is a door painted on the wall.

I know it cannot open.

Still, I sit before it until morning, loving the silver handle, loving the road imagined beyond it, loving even the wall for teaching me desire.

At first light, we leave.

At first light, we remain.

Apple blossom—  
the road passes through it  
and cannot get free.

---

*Scholarly Note.—The six “Appleblossom” pieces are presented as translations from the recently recovered notebooks of Chiri, an otherwise unattested companion of Matsuo Bashō during the poet’s northern journeys. The manuscripts—water-stained, smoke-darkened, and of uncertain provenance—alternate prose observations with brief poems in a hand distinct from Bashō’s. No historical evidence confirms Chiri’s existence; several scholars have suggested that the name, meaning “scattered” or “fallen,” may indicate a fictional traveler, a composite disciple, or the road itself writing in the margins.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, lyrical passage in an earthy American voice about a speaker who longs to be opened by the wind, questions whether wilderness can be home, and imagines a chain of reclamation involving wolves, the Moon, and a white chrysanthemum.
counterfactuals.output:
I want the wind to find the latch in me and worry it loose, to pry my ribs apart like slats on an old corncrib and let the weather walk through. Then maybe I’d know what I belong to. But can wilderness be home, or is home the little lie we hammer together against it?

At dusk, the wolves come down from the black timber and reclaim the road. The road, in turn, reclaims the fields. The fields rise up in foxtail and ironweed and reclaim the abandoned house. The house gives its windows to the Moon, and the Moon, pale thief, gives all that silver back to a white chrysanthemum blooming alone beside the porch.

I kneel there in the dirt, listening. The flower opens without asking who owns the ground. The wind puts both hands inside me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem addressed partly to “Mr. Out-in-the-Woods” and partly to a beloved called “Sweet.” Include beanfields, trees, timberwolves, the Moon, and the question “Who would reclaim me?” Conclude by denying the possibility of either escape or writing a love poem.
counterfactuals.output:
Mr. Out-in-the-Woods, your beanfields keep the dusk like a dark green secret, each row leading farther from the road, each leaf lifting its small, unreadable hand. Beyond them, the trees close ranks. Timberwolves move between their trunks as quietly as old grief, and the Moon hangs above your roof, a white pail emptied of milk. Tell me, if I crossed that field and entered the black timber, who would reclaim me?

Sweet, you are the lamp I carry without light. I speak your name and the branches bend nearer; I remember your mouth and the cold begins. Mr. Out-in-the-Woods says every path belongs to whatever follows it home. Sweet, if the wolves took my shadow, if the Moon wore my face, would you know which silence was mine?

But there is no road out of these woods, no gate beyond the beanfields, no escape at all—and with the trees listening, and Sweet so far away, there is no way to write a love poem.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Invent an “Appleblossom” fragment presented as a loose English translation from the Japanese notebooks of Chiri, Bashō’s traveling companion between *Withered Chestnuts* and *Travelogue of Weatherbeaten Bones*. Let the translation sound eccentric, mystical, playful, and deliberately anachronistic.
counterfactuals.output:
### Appleblossom  
*An apocryphal fragment, loosely translated from the supposed notebooks of Chiri*

Between the book of chestnuts  
and the book of broken weather,  
we misplaced the road.

Bashō blamed the moon.  
I blamed the moon’s small department of maps.

At noon we entered a village where every gate  
had been painted the color of forgetting.  
An old woman sold us tea, three rumors,  
and a password for the next century.

> appleblossom—  
> the mountain uploads  
> one white cloud

“Too modern,” said Bashō.

“Wait,” I answered. “Modernity has not happened yet.”

We slept under a pear tree pretending to be an apple tree.  
All night its blossoms fell upward.  
A fox in a pilgrim’s hat recited the Heart Sutra backward  
and asked whether emptiness accepted foreign coins.

At dawn, my master wrote nothing.

This was his finest poem,  
though later editors ruined it  
by printing the page.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, Whitmanesque prose-poetry meditation on travel and belonging in which the body resembles a reed flute, roads become ruts, nature repeatedly reclaims itself, and the speaker finally realizes that lover and beloved are not separate. Add a brief pseudo-academic attribution at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
I go forth with the continent breathing through me, my ribs the pale reeds of a riverbank, my spine hollowed and fingered by weather, my mouth an aperture through which distance makes its low, unending music; I have called this music departure, though every mile curls backward like smoke toward the first fire, and I have called myself traveler, exile, pilgrim, trespasser, child, though the road beneath my feet becomes ruts, the ruts become runnels bright with rain, the runnels summon sedge and frog-song, and soon the green republic rises again where wheels had sworn dominion. O roads, arrogant scars! Already the root enters you, already the ant carries your gravel away grain by grain, already the goldenrod lifts its many torches through your broken crown. I pass cities whose brick is softened by moss, stations where swallows stitch the rafters to the sky, fences patiently swallowed by vines; I see that nature does not return because she never departed, that beneath each map the earth keeps her older counsel, repeating leaf, flood, feather, rot, blossom, repeating herself not as echo but as appetite. And I too am reclaimed: dust takes my ankles, rain inhabits my hair, the moon lays its cool hand upon my face, and the wind, finding the stops of my reed-flute body, plays a song I had mistaken for loneliness. I thought I traveled toward you, beloved; I thought you waited beyond the salt flats, beyond the black pines, beyond the last inn and the last lamp, separate as a star is separate from the upturned eye. But the farther I went, the more your pulse sounded inside my pulse, the more each stranger wore your inexhaustible countenance, until at the ocean’s margin—where every road loses its name and every rut fills with shining water—I knew the traveler was the road, the breath was the flute, the call was the answering, and lover and beloved were one mouth pouring one breath through the innumerable reeds of the world.

—From the apocryphal *Peripatetic Leaves*, ed. M. Vale, Institute for Imagined Geographies, 1893.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
